title: FFI: extern "C", bindgen, and Zero-Overhead C Interop
prerequisites: Understanding of C functions and structs

progressiveExplaining.eli5: Two countries need to exchange parcels. The rule book (the ABI) says exactly how a parcel must be wrapped so the other country can read it. You declare: 'this incoming parcel is wrapped per the agreement' (extern "C") and then unwrap it in a guarded room (unsafe), because the parcel could be damaged — it wasn't checked by your country's inspectors. A clerk (bindgen) can pre-read the rule book and print the correct wrapping instructions for every parcel type automatically, so you don't write them by hand.
progressiveExplaining.junior: FFI (foreign function interface) lets Rust call C functions: extern "C" { fn strlen(s: *const c_char) -> usize; } and call them inside unsafe blocks. The extern "C" declares the C ABI (calling convention). Use std::ffi::CString to create null-terminated strings, c_char/c_int from std::os::raw. bindgen (a tool) generates Rust declarations from C headers automatically: bindgen header.h -- -I. The generated bindings are used in a build.rs via the bindgen crate. All FFI calls are unsafe (the C side isn't checked by Rust's guarantees). For structs, use #[repr(C)] to match the C layout.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, extern "C" blocks declare foreign functions with the platform C calling convention; the compiler emits a direct call with no marshalling — zero-overhead interop (the call is exactly what C would emit). The ABI must match: types must be FFI-safe (repr(C) structs, C-compatible scalars, pointers), which is checked by the compiler's ffi-safe lint. bindgen parses the C headers (via libclang) and emits Rust items matching the C types/layouts, including enums, unions, and function pointers. All calls are unsafe because the C code may violate Rust's invariants (aliasing, validity). The soundness of the wrapper (the safe API around the FFI) is your responsibility.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The compiler lowers an extern "C" call to a direct machine call following the System V / Windows x64 / AArch64 ABI: arguments in registers/stack per the ABI, return in the return register. No boxing, no conversion — a u32 passes as a u32, a *mut T passes as a pointer. The ffi-safe lint (improper_ctypes) checks that the types in the extern block are FFI-safe (no String, no &T with unknown layout, no enums without repr). bindgen runs at build time (build.rs) using libclang to parse headers and emits the Rust declarations; you link the C library via build.rs (println!("cargo:rustc-link-lib=...")) or the cc crate. Unsafe extern blocks (Rust 2024) make the unsafety explicit: you must write unsafe extern "C" in the 2024 edition.

codeComparison.title: Hand-written extern declarations vs bindgen-generated bindings
codeComparison.summary: Hand-declaring FFI is error-prone (wrong types/layouts); bindgen generates correct bindings from the C headers.

interviewGotchas.question: Why is all FFI unsafe, and what does a sound FFI wrapper need to guarantee?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the safety boundary — interviewers want the invariants the Rust side must uphold when calling unmanaged C code, and how to make it sound.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: FFI calls are unsafe because the C function operates outside Rust's guarantees: it may not follow the aliasing rules (mutating data through a shared reference), may not validate pointers (dangling/null), may assume a different lifetime, or may not be thread-safe. The compiler cannot verify any of this. A sound FFI wrapper is a SAFE function that internally does the unsafe call while upholding the invariants: the input pointers must point to valid, aligned, initialized data for the call duration; the output buffer must have sufficient capacity; the data must not be aliased in a conflicting way; and the C function must not retain the pointers beyond the call (unless documented and handled). The wrapper's doc comments should state the safety contract, and tests (including Miri where possible) should exercise the edge cases. If the C code can be given dangling pointers or overlapping buffers, the wrapper must prevent or document that.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'unsafe just means the call might crash'. Unsafe in FFI is a contract: if you pass a dangling pointer or wrong lifetime, the C code may corrupt arbitrary memory (not just crash), and the corruption may surface in unrelated Rust code. Another trap: assuming the C function is 'trusted' because it's a well-known library — even well-known C libraries have edge cases (null returns, error paths) that violate your assumptions. Candidates who describe the full safety contract show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the C ABI, and why does Rust need #[repr(C)] and extern "C" to interop correctly?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the ABI model — interviewers want the calling convention and layout rules that make direct, zero-overhead calls possible, and the mismatch risks.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: The C ABI defines: (1) the calling convention — how arguments are passed (registers/stack per platform: System V AMD64 on Linux/macOS, Microsoft x64 on Windows, AAPCS on ARM) and how the return value is delivered; (2) the data layout — field offsets, alignment, and padding for structs/unions per C's rules. extern "C" tells the compiler to emit calls using the C calling convention (vs the default Rust ABI, which is unspecified and can differ). #[repr(C)] pins a struct's layout to C's rules (fields in order, C alignment/padding) so the bytes in memory match what the C side expects. If either is wrong — the default Rust ABI for a call, or the default Rust struct layout for data — the interop is silently corrupt: wrong argument positions, wrong offsets, misread fields. Getting both right is what makes the call a direct, zero-overhead machine call with no marshalling.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'extern C and repr(C) are just for style'. They are ABI-correctness requirements; the default Rust calling convention and struct layout are unspecified and may reorder/pack differently. Another trap: thinking FFI is slow (marshalling) — done right, it's a direct call with no overhead; the costs are the unsafe contract and the layout discipline. Candidates who describe the calling convention and layout rules show real depth.
